newsitem.title: CANADA: Five feared dead in Canadian avalanche.
newsitem.headline: Five feared dead in Canadian avalanche.

text.p: As many as five skiers were feared killed in an avalanche on Monday in the mountain wilderness near the Canadian resort of Whistler, British Columbia, police said.

Royal Canadian Mounted Police spokesman Peter Montague said 11 European tourists were heli-skiing on the Phalanx Glacier in the Coast Mountains just outside the bounds of the Blackcomb Mountain ski area. "We think as many as five may have died. We have recovered some bodies, but I don't have confirmation of how many," he said.
Unconfirmed reports from Whistler residents said three bodies had been found.

Rescue teams and helicopters searched for the skiers after the avalanche struck at midafternoon but gave up when night fell, Montague said. A search will begin in earnest on Tuesday morning. He had no further details on where the skiers were from or their identities.
Montague said the avalanche was rated Class Two, which is considered "major" and heavy enough to bury people.

In increasingly popular heli-skiing, skiers are taken by helicopter to remote areas unreachable by lifts and ski down the mountain, usually with a guide. Conditions can be treacherous in the back country where, unlike on developed ski hills, no avalanche control measures are taken. Skiers usually carry locating devices which emit a signal to help rescuers in an emergency.
The weather was clear with a light wind on Monday with temperatures around 16 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 9 Celsius) in the late afternoon, Whistler resort said.

The town of Whistler, about 75 miles (120 km) north of Vancouver, has consistently been rated one of the top ski resorts in North America and attracts many visitors from Europe, the United States and Asia.
